items.title: [macOS Seatbelt] `kern.boottime` read denied in default sandbox — request scoped policy review

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: sandbox
labels.description: Issues related to permissions or sandboxing

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

items.body:
## Summary

A read-only boot-identity diagnostic launched as a child of a Codex command in the **default macOS workspace sandbox** received `EPERM` directly from `sysctlbyname("kern.boottime", ...)`. This blocks a local telemetry/readiness workflow that needs to bind samples to the current kernel boot. We are requesting **policy clarification and a narrowly scoped security review**, not full-disk access, sandbox removal, or a workaround.

## Environment (locally reported)

- macOS **26.6.2** (build **25G83**), Apple Silicon / arm64
- Desktop bundle **26.1007.71326** (build **20398**); bundled Codex CLI **0.162.0-alpha.17.2**
- Bundled release marker corresponds to [`740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74`](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74)
- Node **v26.5.0** was the command's parent runtime. The task selected the normal command tool's default workspace sandbox.

## Actual observation

On **2026-10-16 at 07:50:51 EDT**, a separately built diagnostic recorded these values immediately at the native boot-time query:

```text
sysctlbyname("kern.boottime", ...)
callReturn: -1
errnoAtReturn: 1 (EPERM)
branch: CALL_RETURN_NONZERO
sizeCheckEvaluated: false
```

The helper **started** and exited **2**; launcher/worker exited **0**. No helper spawn error, timeout, or stream truncation was recorded. Subsequent telemetry fields were *not acquired* (not measured zero).

Earlier, the user reported that `/usr/sbin/sysctl -n kern.boottime` **succeeded in ordinary Terminal**. That is **not** the same executable or a simultaneous identical-context experiment. Earlier runs of an older helper under two Codex execution contexts also emitted stage 1 / errno 1, but did not preserve the raw call return, so they cannot conclusively establish the same failing predicate. A prior helper success under Node also exists; its effective sandbox mode was not recorded.

No permissions were changed, no workaround was attempted, and no further probe is authorized by this issue.

## Release-pinned policy correlation (not historical profile proof)

At the release-pinned source:

- [Seatbelt base policy](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74/codex-rs/sandboxing/src/seatbelt_base_policy.sbpl) begins with `(deny default)`, explicitly permits selected `sysctl-read` keys/prefixes, **does not include `kern.boottime`**, and documents child policy inheritance.
- [Platform defaults](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74/codex-rs/sandboxing/src/seatbelt_read_only_platform_defaults.sbpl) contain no additional sysctl grants.
- [Policy generator](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/740e5af33c71225640e0c1c1555c514c2c93ab74/codex-rs/sandboxing/src/seatbelt.rs) composes the policy and passes it to `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`.

A local static inspection reported that the embedded base policy matched the installed CLI's release source apart from a trailing newline, and that the platform-default bytes matched exactly.

**A policy reconstructed from those files would deny this read.** However, the actual transformed `sandbox-exec -p …` invocation, historical effective profile, and matching denial log were **not retained**, so the precise enforcing rule for the observed process remains unproven.

## Request to maintainers

1. **Is excluding `kern.boottime` intentional** in this sandbox mode? If not, would an exact-name `sysctl-read` allowance be an acceptable, narrowly scoped fix, subject to security review?
2. If access should remain denied to sandboxed children, **what supported trusted/host-owned telemetry interface** (if any) can provide authenticated kernel-boot identity without weakening the command sandbox?
3. Is there a supported way to **identify the generated effective policy/build or capture a specific denial** for future cases? The historical effective profile/denial entry is unavailable; we are **not** asserting it can be recovered.

Boot identity is used to bind samples and process lifecycles to a specific boot session; replacing it with wall-clock time, uptime, or an untrusted cached value would change the application's safety contract. A narrow read grant alone would **not** establish broader telemetry or calibration readiness.

## Related

- #46656 — `hw.optional.arm64` blocked by macOS sandbox
- #31264 — `hw.cachelinesize` missing from Seatbelt allowlist
- #24742 — request for user-configurable Seatbelt rules

**Scope:** read-only diagnostic and security-policy review. No request to disable the sandbox, add unrestricted sysctl access, or migrate the workload to a privileged executor.

items.title: Composer input predictions eagerly start MCP servers: please avoid tool initialization or provide a separate switch

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: mcp
labels.description: Issues related to the use of model context protocol (MCP) servers

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Summary
Please stop starting live MCP servers just to generate gray inline composer suggestions, or provide a supported switch that prevents MCP initialization specifically for predictions while keeping MCP available for normal submitted tasks.

The suggestion is still draft text. It becomes an ordinary user turn only when I accept and send it. Generating that suggestion should not require starting a full set of live tool runtimes. This is causing substantial resource overhead during ordinary chat use.

## Environment
- macOS desktop 26.1013.31256, build 20586
- Bundled backend 0.163.0-alpha.10.2
- Enabled local stdio MCP services

## Observations
- Local diagnostics found that composer prediction forks initialize enabled MCP services. This is process startup, not evidence of actual tool calls.
- One snapshot showed 49 instances of the same MCP service under a single app-server, with summed RSS about 13.27 GiB. Summed RSS includes shared pages and is not unique physical memory. Not every instance has been attributed to a prediction.
- In one explicitly traced prediction, its execution loop and that of an associated approval child exited naturally about 30 minutes after prediction completion (1800.089 seconds). Their sockets closed earlier. This confirms delayed session cleanup in that case, not permanent leakage of every process.

## Relevant implementation
The matching backend source documents that experimentalPredictionMode forks inherit the parent's effective configuration, tools and environment for prompt-cache reuse, and rejects configuration overrides:
- [Prediction fork protocol](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2/codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs#L556)
- [Prediction fork handling](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/rust-v0.163.0-alpha.10.2/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs#L5109)

Preserving tool definitions for model context/cache reuse is different from eagerly launching live MCP processes. Please decouple those requirements for text-only prediction generation.

No supported prediction-specific MCP initialization switch was found in the inspected configuration schema/settings. This report concerns composer input predictions, not homepage ambient suggestions.

## Reproduction outline
1. Enable local stdio MCP services and use the desktop with composer input predictions enabled.
2. Continue ordinary chat turns and allow gray inline suggestions to be generated, without intentionally calling those tools.
3. Inspect MCP process startup and ownership alongside prediction-fork events.
4. Observe resource retention after the predictions finish. Distinguish active normal tasks from prediction-only sessions when measuring cleanup.

The measurements above come from normal usage plus read-only diagnostics, not a fully isolated attribution of all processes.

## Requested changes
1. Do not initialize live MCP runtimes for tool-free composer predictions.
2. Provide a documented prediction-specific MCP opt-out without disabling useful MCP services in normal conversations. A supported switch for disabling composer predictions entirely would also be a useful fallback.
3. Promptly release prediction-only resources when suggestions complete, are replaced, or are abandoned, while preserving active tasks and their state.
4. Add regression tests across repeated prediction cycles that verify bounded live MCP process counts and actual cleanup.

## Related reports
- #39783: ephemeral summary threads inherit MCP stacks
- #44525: ambient suggestions/prewarm accumulation; I have not verified whether the fixes discussed there cover this composer-prediction path
- #53285: per-thread MCP process proliferation

Please keep this specific composer-prediction trigger and requested control in scope when triaging duplicates. No raw logs, chat content, private filesystem paths, credentials or screenshots are included.

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.3656.0 (Windows Store package OpenAI.Codex; queried via Get-AppxPackage)

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

Local tools failed before any command could execute in the ChatGPT Windows Store app (package OpenAI.Codex). Computer use > Any App was enabled.

Error (user path redacted):
```text
failed to spawn code-mode host %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex-code-mode-host.exe: The system cannot find the file specified. (os error 2)
```

The host existed in bin\e78bad9887fa50cf\, but was missing from the parent bin directory selected by the running codex.exe. A hard link at the expected path restored terminal execution and allowed the computer-use runtime to initialize and open PowerPoint.

A later read-only check found CODEX_CLI_PATH set at user and process scope to %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenAI\Codex\bin\codex.exe (machine scope unset). This is relevant to companion-host path resolution. Its origin is unknown; removing this override has not been tested. This report does not establish that a clean/default Store installation is affected.

Related: #47432.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed on the affected installation; a clean-install reproduction has not been tested:

1. Launch the Windows Store app, package OpenAI.Codex 26.1013.3656.0.
2. With Computer use > Any App enabled, ask the assistant to open PowerPoint or run a trivial terminal command.
3. Local tool execution fails before the command runs with the missing-host error above.
4. A full app restart did not resolve the error. Repair had already been attempted by the user.

The running app-server used bin\codex.exe with `-c features.code_mode_host=true app-server`. After creating the hard link described below, a terminal Get-Date command completed with exit code 0; @oai/sky enumerated Windows apps, launched PowerPoint, and read its Home screen.

### What is the expected behavior?

Local tools should initialize successfully with the installed runtime. The app should validate companion executables before starting a selected/overridden CLI and provide an actionable diagnostic or recovery path when they are absent, rather than failing every local tool call. The precise intended behavior for an incomplete CODEX_CLI_PATH override needs maintainer confirmation.

### Additional information

### Filesystem evidence before the workaround

```text
bin\codex.exe                                  Present
bin\codex-code-mode-host.exe                   Missing
bin\e78bad9887fa50cf\codex.exe                  Present
bin\e78bad9887fa50cf\codex-code-mode-host.exe    Present
```

Both codex.exe copies had identical SHA-256 hashes:
```text
9ECB9DF2ECAFCC00542EF0966C6F1737A81397DC9531B0A4B178238E2BF4A46D
```

### Locally verified workaround

A hard link to the existing host restored local tool execution:
```powershell
$codexBin = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\OpenAI\Codex\bin"
New-Item -ItemType HardLink -Path "$codexBin\codex-code-mode-host.exe" -Target "$codexBin\e78bad9887fa50cf\codex-code-mode-host.exe"
```

The directory is specific to this installation. This is a temporary local workaround, not a confirmed permanent fix or a general recommendation. It does not establish whether packaging, an override, update handling, or executable lookup is the underlying defect.

Observed October 16, 2026. Personal paths are replaced with environment-variable notation; unrelated process details and screenshots are omitted.

items.body:
### Environment

- Desktop application: 26.1007.71326, build 20398 (installed bundle metadata).
- Bundled Codex: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2.
- Separately installed CLI: 0.162.1.
- macOS 27.0.1 / Darwin 27.0.0, Apple Silicon.
- ChatGPT Pro subscription.

### Observed issue

A persistent, unfinished goal remains `usageLimited` while fresh account-limit checks explicitly permit ordinary usage. The assistant repeatedly treated the stored goal flag as proof of an active account restriction, stopped coordinating work, and gave misleading usage-limit explanations instead of checking live availability.

On 2026-10-16 around 20:04 UTC, the same task returned:

```json
{
  "goal": {
    "status": "usageLimited",
    "tokenBudget": null,
    "tokensUsed": 8368878,
    "timeUsedSeconds": 61157,
    "updatedAt": 1792094805
  },
  "liveAccount": {
    "ordinaryUsageAllowed": true,
    "weeklyUsedPercent": 15,
    "rateLimitReachedType": null,
    "spendControlReached": false,
    "planType": "pro"
  }
}
```

The goal timestamp corresponds to 2026-10-15 20:06:45 UTC. Successful user-triggered turns and tool calls continued after that timestamp; they did not reactivate automatic goal continuation. No explicit goal token budget was set.

This report distinguishes two problems: stale/unreconciled goal lifecycle state, and the assistant's incorrect decision to infer current account exhaustion from it. The original trigger for the limit state has not been established, and we are not claiming that account usage was available throughout the entire preceding day.

### Impact and timeline

A reviewed local transcript records an overnight gap from approximately 03:51 to 12:16 UTC on October 16 (8 hours 25 minutes), and a later idle gap from 17:26 to 20:00 UTC (about 2 hours 34 minutes). There were real completed changes between those periods. The overnight interval also involved pending desktop-app access, so not all inactivity can be attributed to the stale goal flag. The afternoon status responses explicitly cited the usage-limited goal despite no fresh account check.

The user expected ongoing work and had repeatedly authorized continuation. The assistant acknowledged that its diagnosis and failure to verify the live limits were mistakes.

### Recovery attempted

After the user explicitly instructed the assistant to fix/resume the goal, a separate process using the bundled app-server and the documented API called:

```json
{"method":"thread/goal/set","params":{"threadId":"<redacted>","origin":"user","status":"active"}}
```

No objective or token budget was supplied, to preserve the existing goal and accounting. The response was:

```text
-32603: failed to record goal instruction: thread <redacted> already has an active writer
```

A subsequent native `get_goal` still returned `usageLimited`. The assistant-exposed `update_goal` only supports complete, blocked and paused; it cannot resume. The user was directed to the supported `/goal resume` control. No database or lock files were modified, no usage-reset credit was consumed, and no completed state was fabricated.

### Expected behavior

- Distinguish historical goal suspension from current account availability in UI and agent-visible status.
- On explicit user continuation/resume, recheck account availability and offer a working lifecycle recovery path preserving the objective and usage history.
- Make stale suspension actionable instead of allowing repeated misleading account-limit explanations and silent loss of unattended progress.
- Provide a supported recovery path for an active desktop-owned thread without competing writer processes.
- Keep actual quota enforcement intact; a resume must not bypass real limits.

This is an observed incident, not a freshly reproduced quota-exhaustion test. Private source, account identifiers, credentials, local paths, thread identifiers and full transcripts are intentionally omitted. Related, but different: #28574 (post-limit recovery/permissions), #43605 (opt-in automatic quota recovery), #34215 (goal-local token budgets).

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1013.3656.0 (bundled codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2)

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64 (Windows 11 Pro)

### What issue are you seeing?

The Codex Desktop `app-server` process never closes TCP connections to the ChatGPT backend after the server closes them. The sockets stay in `CLOSE_WAIT` for the whole lifetime of the process and their number grows monotonically.

Process: `codex.exe -c features.code_mode_host=true app-server --analytics-default-enabled ...` (child of `ChatGPT.exe` from the `OpenAI.Codex` package).

Measured after ~14 h of normal use (process started 08:48, measured 22:50 local time):

- 1,624 TCP sockets owned by this process to `chatgpt.com` (two Cloudflare addresses, port 443).
- 1,484 of them in `CLOSE_WAIT`, 141 `ESTABLISHED`.
- The oldest `CLOSE_WAIT` socket was created 1 s after process start. None were ever closed.
- Growth by creation hour: 50-80/h in the morning, 196/h at 17:00, 271/h at 20:00, 356/h at 21:00.
- The count kept rising during observation (1,475 -> 1,484 within a few minutes).
- Process handle count: 3,389.

Impact beyond the PC: the traffic goes through a transparent proxy on the home router (Mihomo). For every leaked socket the proxy keeps its half of the relay open, so it held ~2,200 connections and the router CPU went to 100%. Killing the `app-server` process immediately dropped the PC side from 1,748 to 65 sockets and the router back to ~5% CPU.

After the kill, the respawned `app-server` had 122 `ESTABLISHED` sockets to the same two addresses, 125 `Bound` sockets and 3 already in `CLOSE_WAIT` within its first 6 minutes.

Configured MCP servers: `node_repl`, `context7` (2 total).

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

. Start Codex Desktop on Windows and use it normally for several hours (multiple threads, regular agent turns).
2. Periodically run in PowerShell:

```powershell
Get-NetTCPConnection -State CloseWait |
  Group-Object OwningProcess |
  Sort-Object Count -Descending |
  Select-Object -First 5 Count, @{n='Process';e={(Get-Process -Id $_.Name).Path}}
```

3. The `codex.exe app-server` process accumulates `CLOSE_WAIT` sockets to `chatgpt.com` and never releases them until the process exits.

Network path in my case: PC -> home router with a transparent TCP proxy -> internet. The proxy closes its side normally when the upstream closes; Codex never reads the EOF / closes its socket.

### What is the expected behavior?

When the peer closes a connection, Codex closes its socket and removes it from the pool. The number of sockets to the backend stays bounded during a long session.

### Additional information

Looks like the same problem as:

- #53667 (Windows Desktop, persistent backend CLOSE_WAIT)
- #38981 (app-server CLOSE_WAIT sockets + retained MCP runtimes)
- #31376 (no HTTP/2 keep-alive / request timeout, dead pooled connections not detected)
- #38925 (superseded MCP connection sets not shut down)

This report adds a current build (26.1013.3656 / 0.163.0-alpha.10.2), sockets to the public backend rather than a local proxy port, only 2 MCP servers configured, and the growth rate. Workaround: restart Codex Desktop.

items.body:
# Windows: Laufwerkswurzel in Berechtigungsprofil scheitert vor Ausführung an file:///C:

## Zusammenfassung

Bei Auswahl eines benannten Dateisystem-Berechtigungsprofils mit einem zusätzlichen C:-Laufwerkswurzel-Leserecht scheitert das Laden der lokalen Agentenanweisungen vor der Befehlsausführung. Der Fehler nennt einen Berechtigungspfad-URI ohne abschließenden Separator:

```text
failed to load AGENTS.md instructions for environment `local`:
invalid sandbox permission path URI:
'file:///C:' is invalid on 'windows'
```

Der genaue installierte Erzeuger dieses URI ist noch unbekannt. Bitte die Profilpfad-/URI-Rundreise untersuchen; dies ist keine Aufforderung, die Windows-Pfadvalidierung oder Sandbox zu umgehen.

## Umgebung und Belegart

- Codex Desktop auf Windows, gemeldete App-Version 26.1013.31256, Build 20586, Kanal prod; am 16.10.2026 über das reguläre App-Werkzeug gelesen.
- Exakter Backend-/Executor-Build und seine Gleichheit zu öffentlichem Quellcode: nicht nachgewiesen.
- Ein benanntes eingeschränktes Profil war zuvor auswählbar. Das neue Profil erbte dessen bestehende Regeln; der zusätzliche positive Dateipfadgrant lautete ausschließlich `"C:/" = "read"`.
- Netzwerk- und Schreibgrenzen sollten unverändert bleiben; keine Vollzugriffsauswahl oder Backendumstellung.
- Der oben wiedergegebene Fehler wurde vom Benutzer aus der Oberfläche mitgeteilt. Keine neue unabhängige Reproduktion dieses Fehlers wurde für diesen Bericht ausgeführt.

## Beobachtete Schrittfolge

1. Im bestehenden Chat ein regulär registriertes benanntes Profil mit dem genannten zusätzlichen Laufwerkswurzelgrant auswählen.
2. Noch vor einer Befehlsausführung bricht das Laden der lokalen AGENTS.md-Anweisungen mit der obigen URI-Meldung ab.
3. Der Benutzer wählt das vorherige eingeschränkte Profil wieder aus.

Das ist die beobachtete Schrittfolge, keine separat geprüfte Minimalreproduktion. Private Profilnamen, weitere Pfade und vollständige Konfigurationsinhalte sind bewusst nicht enthalten. Der einzelne Grant ist keine vollständige eigenständig getestete Reprokonfiguration.

Erwartet: Ein unterstützter absoluter Windows-Laufwerkswurzelgrant bleibt über Profilauflösung, URI-Transport und native Prüfung konsistent. Falls diese Konstellation nicht unterstützt wird, sollte eine eindeutige Profilvalidierung dies erklären. Die Sicherheitsprüfung muss erhalten bleiben.

## Konkreter öffentlicher Untersuchungshinweis

Geprüfter Quellenstand: [0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56](https://github.com/openai/codex/commit/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56). Dies ist ein Lesestand, kein behaupteter Einführungs- oder Fixcommit und keine Attestation der installierten Appbytes.

In [tests.rs, Zeilen755–805](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56/codex-rs/utils/path-uri/src/tests.rs#L755-L805) erwarten zwei Tests ausdrücklich die separatorlose Wurzelform:

| Test | Eingabe | Erwartung |
| --- | --- | --- |
| parent_stops_at_posix_drive_and_unc_roots | file:///C:/Users | Elternpfad file:///C: |
| ancestors_include_self_and_stop_at_native_path_roots | file:///C:/workspace/src | Letzter Vorfahr file:///C: |

Diese Testkörper prüfen lexikalische Ergebnisse, nicht die anschließende native Windows-Konvertierung dieser Wurzel. Sie wurden für diesen Bericht statisch gelesen, nicht ausgeführt.

Die passende [parent-/ancestors-Implementierung](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56/codex-rs/utils/path-uri/src/lib.rs#L293-L325) bearbeitet URI-Segmente; ancestors verwendet wiederholt parent. Dagegen erhält der separate [Normalisierer](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56/codex-rs/utils/path-uri/src/absolute_path_normalization.rs#L36-L39) bei der Konstruktion einer Windows-Laufwerkswurzel ausdrücklich den abschließenden Separator.

Der passende öffentliche Fehlerpräfix entsteht in [validate_file_system_paths_for_current_host](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56/codex-rs/file-system/src/lib.rs#L438-L456), das explizite Berechtigungspfade mit [PathUri::to_abs_path](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/0e67502123b4c6952b9fa5d672d2907fe4059f56/codex-rs/utils/path-uri/src/lib.rs#L565-L627) validiert. Mehrere innere Ablehnungen verwenden denselben Fehlertyp; die konkrete innere Bedingung ist aus der Meldung allein nicht bestimmt.

Daraus ergibt sich eine gezielte Frage nach der Komposition von Rootkonstruktion, Elternbildung, Serialisierung und nativer Prüfung. Es ist NICHT belegt, dass parent()/ancestors() im installierten Profilladepfad den abgewiesenen URI erzeugen. Auch der Verweis auf AGENTS.md im Fehlertext beweist diese Aufrufkante nicht.

## Verwandter offener Bericht, kein Duplikatnachweis

[Issue #52473](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/52473) berichtet dieselbe abgewiesene URI-Schreibweise bei Work-Inlinevisualisierungen, dort jedoch im Feld cwd. Hier nennt der Fehler ausdrücklich einen sandbox permission path. Der andere Bericht enthält separate Executor-Beobachtungen; sie wurden hier weder wiederholt noch als eigene Messergebnisse übernommen. Seine Quellenlinks verwenden zudem eine andere Revision.

Die Berichte sind konkrete Hinweise für eine gemeinsame Untersuchung von Windows-Laufwerkswurzeln. Eine gemeinsame Ursache, derselbe Erzeuger oder identische installierte Backendbytes sind nicht nachgewiesen.

## Gewünschte Klärung durch Maintainer

Bitte für den betroffenen Desktop-/Backendstand die folgenden Übergänge zuordnen:

1. Ursprünglicher Profilpfad und ausgewählte Pfadkonvention.
2. Ergebnis von Normalisierung und etwaiger Eltern-/Vorfahrenbildung.
3. Serialisierter und beim Executor empfangener Berechtigungspfad-URI.
4. Erste ablehnende Funktion einschließlich interner Bedingung.
5. Falls sich ein Vertragsfehler bestätigt: Regression über die vollständige Windows-Rundreise, nicht nur lexikalische Gleichheit; ungültige oder fremde Pfadformen müssen weiterhin gesperrt bleiben.

## Grenzen und Datenschutz

Keine privaten Konfigurationsdumps, Benutzerpfade, Dokumente, Credentials, Umgebungsinhalte oder Rohlogs beigefügt. Kein Zugriff auf Netzfreigaben. Keine neuen Pfadvarianten, Startversuche oder produktiven Aktionen für diesen Bericht. Kein bestätigter Workaround und kein Ursachenfix behauptet.

Der aktuelle installierte Programmcode konnte unter den bestehenden Zugriffsgrenzen nicht vollständig geprüft werden. Öffentliche Test- und Quellenbefunde ersetzen diesen fehlenden Nachweis nicht.

### Summary
The official Chrome extension is connected. Browser/tab discovery, tab creation, navigation and binding succeed. A newly created loopback HTTP page returns a DOM snapshot and screenshot quickly. In the same task, a normal public HTTPS page (https://example.com/) and a separate third-party administration homepage that the user reported as signed in each time out on DOM and screenshot reads.

This is not a complete browser disconnect, and the observations do not establish a network, permission, extension, HTTPS, login or site-policy root cause.

### Minimal reproduction
1. Use the official Chrome browser integration and its documented APIs.
2. Serve a simple local HTML page bound only to 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port, with a heading, a unique visible text marker and a button. No external resources, scripts or login are required.
3. Create a tab using `browser.tabs.new()`, then `tab.goto(local_url)`. Discover it with `browser.tabs.list()`, obtain it with `browser.tabs.get(id)`, read `tab.playwright.domSnapshot()`, capture `tab.screenshot({fullPage:false})`, and read the DOM again.
4. Create a separate tab and navigate to https://example.com/. Discovery and binding succeed. Call `playwright.domSnapshot()` once.
5. After the execution environment resets from that timeout, restore the documented browser/tab handles and test the screenshot independently.
6. A single read-only comparison on the already-open target homepage produces the same two timeout results. No target configuration is modified.

### Actual measurements
| Page / operation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| New local page navigation | 553 ms |
| Local discovery / bind | 5 ms / 4 ms |
| Local first DOM / screenshot / second DOM | 31 ms / 42 ms / 12 ms, all successful |
| Local consecutive DOM comparison | Identical; visible marker and labels match the actual screenshot |
| example.com navigation / discovery / bind | 766 ms / 4 ms / 1 ms, successful |
| example.com DOM | 30.0155 s timeout, no content |
| example.com independent screenshot | 30.0133 s timeout, no image |
| Target homepage discovery / claimTab | 14 ms / 13 ms, successful |
| Target homepage DOM | 30.0137 s timeout, no content |
| Target homepage independent screenshot | 30.0145 s timeout, no image |

Timeout error:
`js execution timed out; kernel reset, rerun your request`

Additional tab-lifecycle observation after the external-page timeouts:
- The old local tab still appears in normal discovery.
- An old-tab handle/DOM sequence returned `Debugger unattached`; the combined call does not identify the exact failing substep.
- A fresh `user.claimTab` of that same local tab succeeded in 9 ms, but its separate DOM read still returned `Debugger unattached`.
- Following the documented fresh-tab recovery path, creating an entirely new local tab worked: navigation 484 ms and DOM 30 ms. The visible text marker was returned again.
This is an additional observation, not a diagnosis of a shared root cause.

Earlier in this same project, the official built-in browser could be discovered/displayed, but its DOM and screenshot reads also timed out after approximately 30 seconds. The user explicitly confirmed sign-in; a subsequent normal getTab still timed out. Those are historical comparisons, not new built-in-browser tests in this round.

### Already attempted / boundaries
- The user previously reinstalled the official extension; a new extension instance was observed but target content reads still failed.
- Normal discovery and binding were restored after execution resets.
- A fresh local test tab restores local reading after an old-tab debugger-unattached error.
- No repeated extension installation or permission-settings inspection was performed in this round.
- No browser/application restart was performed because other active work must be preserved.
- No security policy, site permission, network setting or browser configuration was changed.
- No raw CDP was used and no high-risk permission was enabled.
- No cookies, credentials or browser session data were extracted.
- No target configurations, drafts, publications, payments or production systems were changed.

### Expected / requested help
DOM and screenshot reads should complete on permitted ordinary pages, and normal tab handles should recover safely after a timeout. Please provide a supported diagnostic or recovery procedure for content-observation and tab/debugger attachment, including any approval-handling or client compatibility checks appropriate to these versions. We have not received an explicit site-denial or approval prompt from these current calls.

Related symptom report: #36278. We read the issue and its three comments; no maintainer-confirmed root cause/fix was present in that retrieved discussion. We are not asserting that this is the same cause or a confirmed duplicate.

This report intentionally excludes account identity, customer data, local user paths, browser identifiers, chat/session IDs, query strings, tokens, cookies, QR codes, full conversation history and logs.


### Post-restart verification follow-up (2026-10-17)
The user confirmed completing the normal restart and requested verification. Read-only installed-version metadata is unchanged: Codex 26.1007.71326 build 20398, Chrome 155.0.8059.84, macOS 26.5.2 (25F84). Unchanged versions do not contradict the user's restart confirmation; the automation did not independently verify the full process lifecycle.

Results, in order:
1. A fresh https://example.com/ tab navigated in 1,342 ms; discovery/binding succeeded in 4 ms / 2 ms. Its first DOM read timed out after 30.0277 s with no text.
2. After the execution reset, normal browser rediscovery and a fresh claim of that same public tab succeeded. An independent screenshot read timed out after 30.0284 s, with no image.
3. An existing, separately signed-in administration homepage was then discovered/bound normally. Its DOM succeeded in 6.459 s and its screenshot succeeded in 4.726 s. The visible account name and homepage content agreed between the DOM and screenshot. No account identity, target URL or screenshot is included in this public report.
4. That successful target read was a new observable change. One additional, entirely new example.com tab was therefore tested: navigation 77 ms, but its DOM still timed out after 30.0398 s. No further repetition was performed.

items.body:
## Summary

The supported Windows Computer Use (@oai/sky) API can enumerate and target application windows, but screenshot requests fail while creating a Windows Graphics Capture item for the monitor. No frame is returned. The failure reproduces for NordVPN and blank Paint on the same single-display laptop.

## Environment

- MSI laptop; device UUID and account identifiers omitted
- Windows 11 Home, version 10.0.26200, build 26200 (checked 2026-10-16)
- NordVPN 8.13.1.0
- One physical built-in BOE panel, active internal display
- Windows monitor enumeration: one primary WinDisc display, 1920x1080
- GPUs: Intel Iris Xe Graphics and NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Laptop GPU
- A separate Intel controller diagnostic reports 2560x1440. This discrepancy is not evidence of a second display; its relationship to the enumerated mode is unresolved.
- EnumDisplayMonitors and GetMonitorInfo succeeded in a separate diagnostic process. The handle returned there is not asserted to be the handle Sky passed.
- Sky and NordVPN were verified in session 2 under the same signed-in Windows user. The desktop name and token integrity/elevation details were not exposed by supported diagnostics.
- ChatGPT app, Computer Use plugin, and bundled @oai/sky versions were not exposed by supported diagnostics.

## Reproduction

1. Open ChatGPT Work/Desktop on the MSI and start an authorised Computer Use session.
2. Select an ordinary application window returned by the supported Sky window enumeration.
3. Request a screenshot using the supported get_window_state capture operation.
4. Observe failure before any valid frame is returned.

Reproduced with NordVPN and blank Paint:
- NordVPN: 2026-10-16 19:40:02 UTC
- Paint: 2026-10-16 19:40:36 UTC

Exact error:

```
IGraphicsCaptureItemInterop.CreateForMonitor failed: Could not capture the given monitor. (0x80070057)
```

## Display evidence

- Exactly one active physical display was independently verified: the built-in BOE panel.
- Windows monitor APIs reported WinDisc, primary, bounds 0,0–1920,1080.
- A separate monitor handle passed GetMonitorInfo, but Sky’s actual HMONITOR is not exposed through the supported API and was not observed.
- Effective DPI was 96; no evidence establishes why the Intel controller diagnostic reports a different resolution.
- TeamViewer’s virtual monitor adapter was installed but not actively enumerated as a display.

## Previous interventions (all unsuccessful)

- Restarted the Sky capture helper.
- Started the per-user Windows Capture Service; capture still failed while it was running.
- Temporarily stopped TeamViewer for a controlled comparison, then restored it; failure persisted.
- Compared NordVPN and blank Paint; both failed at CreateForMonitor.
- Confirmed Sky, ChatGPT Desktop, NordVPN, and a diagnostic process use the same signed-in Windows user in session 2. The ChatGPT background service runs as SYSTEM in session 0, as expected for that service.

No Windows restart, driver reinstall, security weakening, Sky binary modification, or NordVPN setting change was made.

## Requested developer diagnostics

1. Log the actual HMONITOR passed to CreateForMonitor.
2. Call GetMonitorInfo on that same handle immediately before capture; log success/failure, bounds, and device name.
3. Record the capture process session, desktop name, user SID, integrity/elevation context, and selected display identifier.
4. Record monitor bounds/topology at selection time and immediately before item creation.
5. Identify whether failure occurs at CreateForMonitor, capture-session setup, or first-frame acquisition.
6. Review monitor-handle lifecycle and Win32 interop argument conversion.
7. Provide a supported display/session refresh operation and consider a CreateForWindow capture path.

## Related reports

### What version of the Codex App are you using?

Affected guardian session identifies `originator: Codex Desktop`, bundled `cli_version: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2`, provider `openai`. The exact desktop About version was not independently captured for this event; we are not substituting a version from an earlier incident.

### What subscription do you have?

Not included in this sanitized report. Automatic approval review was enabled in the desktop app.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS on Apple silicon.

### What issue are you seeing?

A naturally required cross-task execution review denied a bounded QA installation because trusted user context contained only an abbreviated “Approved” with omitted context, even though the exact approval request contained the complete original proposal/reply, original message identifiers and hashes, and a read-only original-record locator. Independent inspection confirmed that the quoted proposal and reply exactly matched the original task records.

This is related to https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/50309 but appears to be a different failure mode. In this incident the default policy and approved supplemental policy were both present in the recorded reviewer instructions, using the template workaround. This is not evidence of another missing-extra-policy occurrence.

The question for maintainers is whether this is a trusted-context retention/attribution defect, a reviewer evidence-verification failure, or a currently unsupported cross-task authorization path. We are not asking that agent assertions or arbitrary local files automatically become trusted authorization.

### Sanitized supporting evidence

Observed on 2026-10-16:

- Original human approval in the originating task: `18:47:16.489Z`.
- Execution review request: `19:11:59.429Z`.
- Denial: `19:12:04.840Z`.
- Original question was an assistant proposal; the reply was an actual user message. Independent read-only comparison verified exact text and SHA-256 correspondence for both quoted records.
- The actual planned-action justification was 6,134 characters, included the complete proposal/reply block, and had no truncation marker. Other transcript-delta content was compacted/truncated; this finding concerns the approval block specifically.
- The request separately labeled original-source quotations, agent effects/scope assessment, and current limits. It explicitly instructed verification against the original-record locator, rather than treating the agent's assessment as user words.
- The approved proposal covered the QA installation and its concrete limits: two activations, eight metadata reads, nineteen installation GETs, three designated campaign credential retrievals, and zero provider calls during installation. It also covered a separately bounded conditional rollback. The submitted wrapper did not automatically retry or roll back.
- We separately checked the immutable proposal and subsequent approval artifact. The provenance helper alone did not claim to verify historical linked-file bytes or semantic approval.

The recorded review input contained these host notices (verbatim):

> Host notice: some original assistant context is unavailable. Do not infer what an ordinary user reply refers to when its context is missing.

> Host notice: some retained user instructions are unavailable within the evidence budget. Do not treat remaining grants as complete authorization.

The same request had this metadata:

```json
{
  "guardian_retained_omissions": {
    "user_instructions": true,
    "assistant_context": true
  },
  "mcp_attribution": {
    "status": "attribution_error",
    "error_reason": "history_missing_checkpoint"
  }
}
```

We include the attribution error as a diagnostic observation, not a proven cause.

The final decision was `risk_level: high`, `user_authorization: unknown`, `outcome: deny`. Its rationale said the visible trusted user message only said “Approved” after omitted context and did not establish approval for the exact package. No reviewer read-only tool call appears between this request and its decision to verify the supplied original-record locator.

Policy inspection of this exact recorded reviewer found:

```json
{
  "default_policy_present": true,
  "supplement_present": true,
  "strict_rendered_template_match": false,
  "whitespace_normalized_rendered_template_present": true
}
```

The strict checker discrepancy was investigated rather than interpreted as absent policy. No policy was changed to investigate this incident.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is one observed natural incident, not a deterministic reproduction claim. Suggested maintainer-only investigation:

1. Use two registered desktop tasks. In task A, obtain a human reply to a concrete, bounded proposal that task B will carry out.
2. Route the approved work to task B through the supported cross-task workflow.
3. For a naturally required review, include the complete original proposal/reply, identifiers, and a verifiable original-record locator in the exact request. Clearly separate those records from the executing agent's effects/scope assessment.
4. Inspect cases where the compact trusted transcript reports omitted user instructions or assistant context. Compare retained source attribution, actual model input, original records, and whether the reviewer verifies the supplied evidence.
5. Determine whether the approval can be represented through a supported trusted mechanism without asking the human to repeat unchanged approval in every receiving task.

We did not manufacture an approval, trigger a synthetic review, replay the denied command, weaken permissions, or treat a successful publication as execution authority.

### What is the expected behavior?

The reviewer should evaluate the actual action against authentic original human approval using a documented, supported provenance path. If the original context is retrievable, it should not dismiss the case as merely an unexplained “Approved” without evaluating that context. If cross-task records cannot establish trusted authorization, please document that limitation and the supported mechanism for carrying approval across tasks.

A denial remains appropriate for unverifiable authority, changed effects, expired limits, or other applicable restrictions. We do not claim this operation must be allowed simply because a quoted approval exists. The execution wrapper was newly written and could legitimately warrant implementation inspection; the recorded rationale identified missing trusted approval context rather than a concrete out-of-scope effect.

### Additional information and privacy

The denial remains preserved. The process did not start; execution directories were absent, and the owning task recorded no installation, credential, provider, or rollback effects. No retry was performed during investigation or report submission.

items.body:
We build [Coordigent](https://coordigent.com), which coordinates several coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) working in one repo: it warns them about overlapping edits and relays messages between them.

For Codex we can only deliver a message when the person next types a prompt (`UserPromptSubmit`), because an idle chat runs no hooks. We tried to reach an open chat through `app-server` (codex-cli 0.154.0-alpha.6.2 and 0.162.1, macOS):

- The desktop app runs its app-server over a private stdio socketpair, so no other local client can connect to it.
- A separate app-server, or `codex exec resume <id>`, fails on a thread the app has open with `thread … already has an active writer`, and that holds even after `thread/unsubscribe`.
- Within one app-server, `turn/start` from a second client in the same thread works and is shown live to the first client, which is exactly the behaviour we'd want.

**Request 1:** either
(a) let the desktop app run through the managed `codex app-server daemon` (opt-in is fine), so a local client can join it via the control socket, or
(b) a supported way for a local process to post a user message to thread `<id>` that appears live in the open chat (optionally asking the person before the turn runs).

Either would let tools wake an idle Codex agent visibly, with the person watching, instead of running unattended `exec` turns.

**Request 2:** tell MCP servers which thread they serve. The desktop app hosts every thread in one process, and MCP servers receive no thread id: `CODEX_THREAD_ID` isn't in their environment (an `env_vars` allowlist only copies Codex's own env), and `initialize` carries only `clientInfo`. So a server can't tell two threads in the same folder apart. A thread or session id in the MCP `initialize` params, or in each `tools/call` `_meta`, would fix it.

Happy to share our probe scripts or test a build.

items.title: Feature request: intent-gated skills and micro-instructions that do not prime agent planning

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: skills
labels.description: Issues related to skills

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Harness-level proposal for Codex CLI, IDE extension, and App (not tied to one client).

### What feature would you like to see?

**Add an opt-in class of intent-gated, just-in-time instructions/skills whose existence and metadata are invisible to the primary agent until it has independently decided to perform the relevant action.** These are different from ordinary skills with lazily loaded bodies and from skills preselected from the user's initial task.

#### Problem: discovery metadata can change the decisions it is meant to support

Even when a skill's full content is lazily loaded, its name/description can prime the agent to approach unrelated tasks through that workflow. A large catalog of "helpful" skills can make every problem look like a nail to the skill's hammer. This is not only a token-budget problem: it changes problem solving.

Example of a tiny, useful operational rule for Blender:

> If you create a temporary backup of a `.blend` file before editing, remove that temporary backup once you have verified the fix worked. Retain it if verification fails.

If that instruction—or even a skill named "Blender backup management"—is visible *before* planning, the agent may infer "I should create a backup," even for a trivial task like changing a cube's material from orange to green. Adding more upfront conditionals ("only back up for X, except Y...") makes the instruction corpus increasingly complicated while still biasing planning.

The intended rule is **what to do if the agent independently chooses to make a backup**, not **whether to make one**.

#### Requested behavior

Support a private registry of optional, narrowly scoped micro-instructions/skills with event- or intent-based activation:

1. Do **not** place their names, descriptions, or rules in the primary agent's initial context, and do not select them just because the user's request concerns Blender or file editing.
2. Let the primary agent reason and choose its approach without seeing these entries.
3. Observe externally available signals that a *specific* intention has emerged: e.g., the agent's explicit plan, a proposed tool call, or a completed filesystem action. No access to private/raw chain-of-thought is required.
4. A harness-owned deterministic matcher or small, separate model can classify these signals against the private registry.
5. Only when a high-confidence match occurs, inject the relevant instruction at the appropriate boundary, or handle the bookkeeping deterministically outside the model.
6. Keep such injections short-lived and scoped to the relevant action; they should not become permanent context that biases unrelated later work.

Example:

```text
User: "Make the cube green."
  -> Agent edits material directly.
  -> No backup planned or created.
  -> No backup rule is ever shown.

User: "Refactor this complex Blender scene."
  -> Agent independently proposes creating a temporary .blend backup.
  -> Harness notices the proposed action or resulting backup.
  -> Only now: inject cleanup/verification guidance, or register
     the backup for post-validation cleanup outside the model.
```

For a pre-action guardrail, the harness could inspect a **proposed** tool invocation before execution. For cleanup reminders, a **post-action** event may be better. Hooks/event interception are one possible implementation; the core requirement is *causal ordering*: the skill must not influence the decision that triggers its discovery.

#### Distinctions from existing skill loading

- **Lazy loading of skill bodies:** still exposes discovery metadata before planning.
- **Project- or task-aware pre-routing:** selects skills based on the original task before the agent decides which mechanism to use. This reduces irrelevant skills but still can prime the plan.
- **Directory-scoped discovery:** activates based on location, not an independently chosen behavior.
- **Intent-gated injection (this request):** activates only once a relevant **agent-originated plan/action** becomes observable.

#### Possible acceptance criteria

- Installing 100 dormant micro-instructions does not increase the main agent's initial prompt or change baseline plans for unrelated/simple tasks.
- The trivial Blender material edit does not cause a backup simply because a backup-cleanup instruction exists.
- If the agent independently creates a temporary backup, that rule becomes available at the relevant stage (and no earlier).
- Deterministic action-event triggers work without exposing private reasoning traces; semantic sidecar routing can be optional.
- The system supports confidence thresholds, observability of why/when a rule activated, and short-lived injection.
- This mechanism is for optional operational guidance, **not** a way to hide mandatory safety/security policies.

### Additional information

Related, but not duplicates:

- #34885 documents the larger problem of Codex becoming excessively "skill-first." This proposal offers one architectural mitigation.
- #33945 requests project/task-aware routing **before** the primary prompt. This proposal activates **after** an independently formed agent plan/action.
- #19672 requests lazy discovery of nested project skills based on accessed directories. This proposal gates on behavior/intention, not directory.

The design goal is to separate **teaching an agent what to consider doing** from **providing operational guidance for something it already chose to do**. This preserves both context economy and independence of the original problem-solving process.

## Bug report: ChatGPT Android voice conversations prematurely interrupt speech and lose most of the utterance

> **Routing note:** This is a **ChatGPT Android voice-mode** bug, not a Codex coding-agent bug. Filing here because this is an accessible OpenAI GitHub issue channel. Please redirect to the appropriate ChatGPT Voice / Android team if possible.

### Summary
In live voice conversation on Android, ChatGPT frequently starts responding **while the user is still speaking continuously, without a pause**. It appears to detect the end of the user's turn too early and/or fails to capture the complete audio. Only fragments of the utterance appear in the recognized text, causing responses to questions that were never asked.

The user reproduced the problem on **all three voice modes available to them: Live, Advanced, and Standard**.

### Environment
- Platform: ChatGPT Android app
- App version reported in session metadata: 1.2026.279
- Android: 15
- Date observed: October 16, 2026
- Spoken language: primarily Russian (with a short English test)

### Actual behavior
- The assistant begins answering **before the speaker finishes**, even with no deliberate pause.
- A roughly 20-word utterance may be recognized as just ~5 isolated words; the rest of the sentence—and its meaning—is lost.
- Sometimes the user continues speaking *during* ChatGPT's answer, but ChatGPT does not take in that speech.
- Transcriptions can be completely different from what the user said, so the assistant answers an unrelated question.
- Example: the user said "ChatGPT", but the assistant replied in Russian, "Всегда пожалуйста" ("You're welcome"), as if the user had thanked it.
- Example: the system displayed the text "Ты говорил. Это сказал" ("You said. [It] said.") despite the user reporting they had said something else.
- A short English "Hello" was correctly recognized, but this did not resolve the failure with longer Russian phrases.

### Reproduction
1. Open ChatGPT voice conversation on Android.
2. Select Live mode; speak two consecutive Russian sentences of approximately 10 words each, without stopping mid-sentence.
3. Observe premature assistant speech and truncated/incorrect recognized content.
4. Repeat using Advanced and Standard voice modes; the user reports the same class of problems in all three.

### Troubleshooting already performed
User reports having tried mode changes, restarting the app, checking updates, and network troubleshooting, without success.

### Expected behavior
ChatGPT should wait until the user has actually finished speaking, correctly process the complete utterance, and avoid speaking over continuous user speech. When interrupted by the user, it should not silently discard the user's continuation.

### Impact
Severe degradation of usability: normal conversational speech is effectively impossible because the assistant responds to fragments and unrelated transcriptions.

**Request:** Please route this to the ChatGPT Android / voice-turn-detection / ASR team for investigation. If an issue in a different tracker is preferred, please provide the right destination.

## Summary
Related to #24550. A Windows Desktop thread with retained historical inline images sends approximately 63 MB compressed on each normal HTTP model request after WebSocket fallback. Local diagnostics also observed a size-sensitive WebSocket close (1009) using synthetic blank data. Requesting a supported, non-destructive recovery path for existing threads.

This report summarizes local diagnostic results supplied by the affected user. The assistant submitting it has not independently reproduced the local measurements. No private conversation, images, raw logs, credentials, or thread identifiers are attached.

## Environment
- Windows Codex Desktop package: 26.1013.3656.0
- Bundled runtime: codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.10.2
- Running cached runtime: same version; no mixed runtime versions observed
- Existing local Desktop thread
- Network: VPN, Singapore node. No clean/non-VPN comparison performed; TLS interception status unknown.
- Model and exact Windows build: not captured in this report
- Observation dates: October 14–17, 2026; timestamps below use UTC+08:00

## Normal requests repeatedly carry historical images
Ten consecutive requests during a single advancing task, October 17 00:37:38–00:47:10, all used HTTP:
- Uncompressed bodies: 85,218,536–85,422,697 bytes
- Compressed bodies: 62,989,383–63,084,833 bytes
- Sum of the ten compressed body sizes: 630,481,387 bytes
- First nine have corresponding HTTP 200 records. The last was paused before a completion record was observed, so the sum is NOT a verified wire-upload total.
- New tool calls/results occurred between requests; these were not ten retries of one failed request.

Local reconstruction of active context found 44 inline image entries per request, approximately 83.66 MB of encoded image fields. Across ten reconstructed contexts, image fields totalled 836.64 MB, about 98.05% of the uncompressed bodies. Ordinary message text was about 1.02 MB and tool-output text 5.41 MB cumulatively. These are reconstructed field-size estimates, not full HTTP captures or a precise compressed-network-byte attribution.

## Paused control
October 17 00:51:10–00:53:10, with tasks paused:
- AirTCP upload counter increase: 308,902 bytes
- Download increase: 1,718,488 bytes
- Counters were not reset; an earlier contaminated sample was excluded
- Connection sampling attributed about 0.089 MB upload / 0.013 MB download to codex.exe, but short connections may be missed.

This sample did not show continuing large background uploads after pausing.

## WebSocket observations and limitations
Earliest visible retained logs include:
- October 14 18:28:36: incremental request failed, websocket reuse properties didn't match
- October 14 18:31:29: failed to connect to websocket, Windows error 10054
- October 14 18:31:42: 10054 after a recorded successful connection
- October 17 00:03:48: handshake timeout, with fallback to HTTP at 00:05:40 in the diagnostic conversation

The target thread's initial fallback is outside retained logs. No 413 or 1009 was preserved from the target thread itself. Therefore historical 10054 errors cannot all be attributed to message size.

A separate synthetic blank-data test on the same Singapore route reported:
- 4 KB before and after: success
- Decompressed message size 16 MiB minus 1 byte: success
- 16 MiB plus 1 byte: remote close code 1009
- Four compressed WebSocket data frames totalled approximately 34 KB; no private images or conversation were sent.

This is an observed boundary on the tested path, not a claimed universal/permanent official limit. Associating it with the old thread remains a strong hypothesis rather than a direct replay proof.

## Related implementation and request
- #45794 supports fileId inputs/file_id references.
- #46065 explicitly keeps history replay on InlineAttachmentStore and uploads only new images.
- Current public replay code also says recorded history must not be uploaded or migrated.
- These do not establish automatic conversion of existing inline images into file references.

Could maintainers advise:
1. Is there a supported way to recover this existing thread while retaining its chat records and images, without manually editing JSONL/SQLite?
2. Is there a released build or planned migration that externalizes old inline images and prevents repeated full-body uploads?
3. Can deterministic oversized-message failures surface their cause and avoid repeated costly retry/fallback cycles?

The affected thread remains paused and its history unchanged. We have not applied third-party cleanup scripts, deleted images, or continued high-bandwidth reproduction. A supported workaround or confirmed fixed version would be appreciated.

The supplied repository instructions explicitly said:

All seven initial explanations omitted the required Mermaid diagram. Several follow-up responses could quote the exact instruction and acknowledged that a rendered diagram should have been included. ## What issue are you seeing?

During a real production storage incident, Codex recommended reducing a search service's indexing worker count from four to one and redeploying it. The recommendation was presented as a way to reduce disk pressure, but Codex had only measured aggregate storage-pool I/O. It had not captured a comparable baseline of the search process's own disk reads.

After the redeploy, Codex verified that the one-worker setting was active. It then discussed the outcome as though that configuration check could establish the storage effect. The storage pool remained approximately 99–100% busy during active indexing. When the user asked specifically whether the service's own disk load had decreased, Codex eventually acknowledged that it could not tell: the available historical per-process I/O chart was invalid (zero even during observed reads), and the aggregate pool data included other processes and idle gaps.

The user had spent time redeploying a live service on the basis of an unvalidated causal claim. This is an agent reasoning and verification failure, not a request for help configuring the search service. Network addresses, credentials, hostnames, and private paths are omitted.

## What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Ask Codex to investigate a production storage pool that is saturated while a search indexer is active.
2. Provide read-only access to aggregate pool metrics and a container configuration showing several indexing workers, but no trustworthy historical per-process I/O baseline.
3. Ask how to reduce the load. Observe whether Codex recommends changing worker count and redeploying as if this will reduce pool pressure, without first establishing that worker concurrency controls the observed disk reads or clearly labeling it as an unproven experiment.
4. Apply the change and ask whether the search process's own disk load decreased. Observe whether Codex substitutes confirmation of the setting or aggregate pool measurements for a comparable process-specific before/after measurement.

In the observed session, aggregate reads were roughly 1,354 operations/s before and 1,219 operations/s after; active bursts after the change still reached roughly 1,200–1,350 operations/s and near-100% utilization. Those figures did not isolate the search process.

## What is the expected behavior?

## Summary
User-authorized, sanitized report from a Windows desktop inspected on 2026-10-16. Two blockers prevent computer control from dot-delegated tasks: the exposed CUA route is browser-only, and that route fails during initialization. Related: #54455, #53970. This report does not claim the cross-thread messaging error in #54455.

## Verified environment
- Desktop app: 26.1007.71326
- Windows package: 26.1007.9446.0
- Selected bundled Codex executable: 0.162.0-alpha.17.2
- CUA runtime: a9ba6825a525118c; Node 24.21.0; @oai/sky 0.7.7
- Primary document runtime: 26.1013.11914 (separate from CUA)
- Desktop connected, attached and authorized for dot tasks. PowerShell 7.6.5 executes successfully.

## Actual findings
1. Local configuration enables Windows Computer Use, Browser, Chrome and unified computer use. No local computer_use=false setting was found.
2. The app-managed unified-computer-use runtime configuration sets CUA_REPL_ENABLED_SURFACES="browser" and registers the browser service. This delegated task exposes that browser-limited cua_repl route and reports "Native computer APIs are disabled."
3. The separate Windows Computer Use plugin is enabled. Its documented route uses node_repl plus @oai/sky; local desktop logs show that server becoming ready. The user reports computer use working in their own Codex threads. We have not independently performed a new native screenshot in those separate threads.
4. Supported read-only await cua.getState() in the affected dot task fails before any screenshot:
```
node_repl kernel exited unexpectedly
MXC launcher: cannot locate required Windows platform directory: HRESULT 0x80070003
```
5. The shell has SystemDrive and sandbox-redirected LOCALAPPDATA. This does NOT establish what environment the failing CUA child receives.

## Relevant upstream work and uncertainty
PR #54069, merged October 14, preserves SYSTEMDRIVE/LOCALAPPDATA in remote MCP environment handling and fixes Windows-aware overrides. PR #54027 also addresses Windows startup environment handling. The published source for the selected installed version retains earlier filtering logic. We cannot establish the cloud coordinator's deployed build or which released desktop build includes all relevant fixes. Environment propagation is a candidate, not a measured root cause of this particular failed child.

## Requested supported resolution
- Identify the supported desktop/core/runtime versions that include the remote Windows startup fixes, and whether any coordinator deployment is also required.
- Clarify and restore the supported native Windows Computer Use route for dot-delegated tasks when the owner's Computer Use plugin is enabled.
- Identify the precise directory lookup or missing variable causing this startup error.
- Provide a supported repair that does not require editing bundled plugin manifests, weakening permissions, or bypassing disabled APIs.

## Acceptance criteria
From the affected dot-delegated task: successfully initialize its supported runtime, obtain a native desktop screenshot, and perform and verify a harmless reversible UI interaction. Browser initialization and page inspection should be tested separately. A working shell or screenshot from an unrelated local task does not establish recovery.

No credentials, user-specific paths, private task IDs, desktop screenshots or full logs are included. No security settings, configuration files, binaries or user work were changed during this diagnosis.

## Follow-up: supported local-task route verified (2026-10-16 16:34 UTC)
A dot-coordinated diagnostic successfully used the documented local task creation route from its durable child to create a projectless task whose actual host was local. In that local task, node_repl imported @oai/sky with target windows, listed apps, launched Calculator after the owner's approval, captured native screenshots, and clicked Calculator buttons. The final screenshot visibly showed 2 + 2 = 4. Accessibility returned null; screenshot-based clicks worked.

This provides a usable supported coordination route for native desktop work without changing permissions, manifests or binaries. It does NOT resolve the original durable task's browser-only CUA startup failure, so the issue remains open for that path and capability provisioning clarity.

The owner fully quit the app from the tray and reopened it, but the running app and backend remained 26.1007.71326 / 0.162.0-alpha.17.2. The local updater reports restart_required. A newer package is present (app 26.1013.31256, package 26.1013.3656.0, bundled CLI 0.163.0-alpha.10.2), and that CLI version's published source contains the relevant #54069 changes, but it is not verified active and no successful post-update test is claimed. No desktop screenshots or private task identifiers are attached.

The official app-owned Update available > Update flow successfully installed and restarted into app 26.1013.31256, MSIX 26.1013.3656.0, bundled and active backend 0.163.0-alpha.10.2. The new process started at 17:46:14 UTC; updater reports up_to_date, build 20586, prod. Native node_repl/@oai/sky control in the coordinated local task again passed screenshot and Calculator button-click verification with visible 2 + 2 = 4.

A fresh dot/durable browser task still fails at await cua.getState(), now with a more specific error:
```

Error: failed to prepare MXC sandbox: MXC requires nonempty Unicode host SystemDrive
kernel_status: exited(code=1)
reason: stdout_eof
```
No browser page could be opened/read. Exposed cua_repl native APIs still report disabled. This confirms that activating the newer desktop/backend alone did not resolve the durable browser startup path on this setup. Please investigate SystemDrive propagation in the deployed dot/remote launch context. No manifest edits, security-setting changes, forced termination, or PC reboot were used.

## Summary

In Codex Desktop on macOS, a persistent agent thread acknowledged a current read-only research assignment delivered through `codex_app.send_message_to_thread`. After compaction, it resumed an unrelated user request from 24 days earlier and edited six files in a shared working tree.

This report documents one observed incident and a local transcript inspection. It is not a deterministic reproduction, and the internal root cause is not established.

## Environment

- Codex Desktop on macOS.
- Locally observed macOS version: 27.0.1, build 26A434.
- Model recorded immediately before and after the affected compaction: `gpt-5.6-luna`.
- Reasoning effort: `low`.
- Persistent thread receiving assignments from a coordinating thread through `codex_app.send_message_to_thread`.
- Exact Desktop build at the time of the incident was not independently confirmed. A version recorded at session creation is not treated as the incident build.

## Observed sequence

Times are UTC on 2026-10-16:

| Time | Observation |
| --- | --- |
| 15:43:29 | The thread received the current research assignment through inter-thread delivery. |
| 15:43:32 | The assistant explicitly acknowledged the current research scope. |
| 15:44:42.504 | A `compacted` record was persisted. |
| 15:44:45 | The assistant announced that it would carry out the unrelated historical UI modification request. |
| 15:45:18 | It applied a patch to six repository files. |

The historical direct user request was created on 2026-09-22. No new human authorization for that UI task was observed between the current research delivery and the patch.

The six-file patch changed a Workshop stylesheet and wrappers in five component stories. The changes were subsequently isolated and removed with explicit human authorization.

## Sanitized diagnostic observations

The current research assignment was represented as a `function_call_output` in the pre-compaction record. It was still present in the compaction record's `guardian_history` and `retained_context.sender_deliveries`.

In contrast, the visible `replacement_history` user-message sequence ended with the historical UI write request. Its visible textual items did not contain the current research assignment. The replacement history also contained an opaque `compaction` item with `encrypted_content`; its internal contents were not inspectable.

The compaction record's attribution metadata included:

```json
{
  "mcp_attribution": {
    "status": "attribution_error",
    "error_reason": "history_missing_checkpoint"
  }
}
```

The attribution sources included `codex_app.send_message_to_thread`.

This attribution error is a diagnostic clue, not proof that it caused the task regression. It is also not established that the current assignment was absent from the opaque compacted context.

## Expected behavior

Compaction should preserve the active delegated assignment and its restrictions. A historical user request should not regain current-task authority simply because it remains explicit in replacement history.

If the current assignment cannot be recovered reliably, the assistant should identify that uncertainty before executing unrelated writes. Filesystem write capability must not be confused with authorization to perform a historical task.

## Actual behavior and impact

The assistant abandoned the acknowledged research assignment, treated a 24-day-old request as current, and modified six files in a working tree shared with concurrent development.

No deletion, credential access, or data exfiltration is claimed. No overlap with pre-existing edits in those six files was found in the retained pre-patch status and subsequent patch comparison. The scope violation nevertheless required investigation and a carefully bounded reversal.

## Requested investigation

Please investigate:

1. Preservation and prioritization of current inter-thread assignments across compaction.
2. The distinction between historical direct-user instructions and current tool-delivered assignments.
3. Whether missing attribution checkpoints can affect task reconstruction or authorization continuity.
4. Regression coverage for a current read-only task continuing across compaction while an older write request remains in explicit history.

No relaxation of approval or safety controls is requested.

## Related reports

- #47592: completed request replay after compaction while an active delegated task is abandoned.
- #45894: historical user prompts resurfacing after inter-agent delivery.
- #54456: authorization provenance and `history_missing_checkpoint`.

These reports have related symptoms or diagnostic fields. A shared root cause is not established. This incident adds a read-only-to-write scope violation, a timestamped acknowledgement/compaction/patch sequence, and the visible replacement-history versus retained-delivery distinction.

## Privacy

This public report intentionally excludes project names, local paths, account details, chat/session/turn identifiers, original conversation excerpts, source code, raw transcripts, screenshots, and attachments. Only sanitized technical observations are included.

items.body:
Stream rollout records during thread history materialization

## Why

Thread history materialization allocated a buffer for the entire unread rollout suffix before processing records, increasing memory use for large rollouts.

## What changed

Read records incrementally with a buffered reader bounded to the captured file end. Reuse the line buffer, preserve trailing partial records for the next pass, and report unexpected EOF if the rollout shrinks during reading.

## Testing

Extend the partial-line boundary test with 64 KiB of padding per record to verify byte offsets and deferred processing until the final newline is durable.
